speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head Q of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Digitalisation is transforming how people live, work, play and interact.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Business enterprises must embrace it to remain relevant.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Our future is being shaped by digitalisation in ways unimaginable and at a pace unprecedented.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: As a result of the digital economy, many of our top companies in the world are now in the technology space.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: It is clear that our Government, businesses and workers must look to digitalisation to transform our economy, create opportunities and move up the value chain.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: That way, we stay relevant and create good and enduring jobs.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: If done well, we can turn our vulnerabilities into opportunities.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Traditional factors of production like land, labour, capital, or even our ageing population, are no longer hard constraints in the digital economy and, if we play our cards right, we can be successful.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: However, digitalisation does bring about many challenges, especially for a city-state with a small population and a consumer base.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Data analytics, machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI) require massive amounts of data.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: For our Government and local enterprises alike, it would be challenging to acquire a large enough volume of data, compared to other larger countries.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: How we overcome this constraint would make a big difference in our digitalisation success.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: If there are more such agreements, with a framework for sharing aggregate anonymised data, for mutual recognition or for interoperability, it would be beneficial to Singapore as well as all participating economies.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Even as data are shared with our local business enterprises, we would need to consider issues like personal data privacy and, therefore, the principles upon which data requests by private enterprises can be agreed to or not by the Government.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: This is an issue that needs clarity and could the Minister also inform us of what these principles are?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Digital talent alone is not sufficient for innovation.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Often, design thinking and deep insights into specific industry are also needed for successful innovations and commercialisation.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) has a Design Thinking Unit.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: How would the Ministry increase this Unit's impact for innovation and commercialisation in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Just as we set boundaries in the area of Bioethics, we would similarly need to set up an ethical framework within which AI can operate here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Can the Minister advise us on the work around this area as well?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: One of the key success factors for digitalisation is scale and capacity.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Unfortunately, this is a challenge for many of our small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: How would MCI induct and incentivise such SMEs to take on digitalisation for a brighter future for themselves?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: There is also a pressing need as we become more digital as a nation to enhance our cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I will address this issue under a different cut later.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Chairman, as an interim measure to augment Singaporeans as Singapore embarks on digitalisation, we hear a clarion call from the industry that there is a dearth of digital talent in data science and cybersecurity, computer science and so forth.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: And as we transform our economy, such talents would be in very high demand.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The Government Technology Agency (GovTech) actively recruits talents in the Technology Industry to turn our Smart Nation vision into a reality.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: On the other hand, due to scarcity of such talent, GovTech would be competing with the private sector for similar talents.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: How would we strike the right balance here, such that we create a symbiotic relationship between the private and public sectors instead of creating a "win-lose" situation amounting to a "zero sum" game?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: What are the projections for such graduates in the next five to 10 years?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: That way, we can attract more investments into Singapore now which will eventually benefit future Singapore graduates in such fields.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: The alternative is to risk such investments going elsewhere.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Over the years, the Government has been urging companies, including SMEs, to transform and adopt appropriate technology to stay relevant and competitive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This message appears to have sunk in and there is keen awareness of the need to go digital.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, awareness may not necessarily translate into action as a number of companies, especially the smaller businesses, have been slow to make the transition.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Minister Iswaran, at MCI's workplan seminar last year, said that it is not about a lack of awareness or will on SMEs’ part anymore but more about them being resource-constrained and lacking capacity to get the transformation done.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Similar observations were also made by the Chief Executive Officer of Singapore Business Federation (SBF), Mr Ho Meng Kit, in a commentary last year.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: He mentioned that business transformation is hindered by talent deficit in Singapore's tech sector and the cost or perceived cost of adopting digital solutions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the commentary, Mr Ho gave several suggestions to businesses to tackle the tech gap, for example, by leveraging the Infocomm Media Development Authority's (IMDA’s) SMEs Go Digital Programme.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: SBF called on the Government to build on the momentum with robust measures that encourage, support and strengthen the digitalisation and research and development efforts of companies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In reviewing the developments over the years, what is the assessment on the effectiveness of our initiatives in digitalising companies?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Are we better able to appreciate the specific challenges faced by SMEs and address them?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How do we intend to continue helping companies access opportunities and scale in the Digital Economy?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is encouraging to hear and it should remain our priority to accelerate digital transformation in order to create new opportunities, both locally and in the region.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For an SME to go digital, talent is paramount.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the competition for talents in fields, such as automation and machine learning, is fierce.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Our SMEs may be no match for multinational corporations (MNCs) when it comes to recruitment.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One of the key challenges to any digitalisation faced by SMEs is getting all their employees ready and equipped for these changes.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: A chain is only as strong as its weakest link.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In relation to cybersecurity jobs, as advertised by the Professional Conversion Programme (PCP) on Workforce Singapore's (WSG's) website, residents have given me feedback that it is difficult to get a place into such professional conversion programmes.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This issue is that these programmes are on a place-and-train basis.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Place-and-train means that they need to get a job first before they can get training.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These residents are stuck in a catch-22 situation.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The creation of jobs for Singapore in the ICM sector is contingent on Singapore being an attractive hub to local and global businesses.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And how do we ensure that research, innovation and entrepreneurship continue to be our engines of growth?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Talents are critical in building new and successful industries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We need a high concentration of skilled workers with a critical mass of world-class talents to attract top enterprises and future unicorns to Singapore to create good jobs, and we need to develop Singaporeans to excel in these jobs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As talents beget talents, there is a virtuous cycle to this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What other efforts are in place to help Singaporeans switch careers and stay meaningfully employed in the digital economy?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How can enterprises that are less tech-savvy but keen to transform, better access and tap into this pool of reskilled and upskilled workers?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As Singapore continues on our relentless pursuit to reskill and upskill our Singaporean Core, it can be expected that enterprises will look to topping up their teams with overseas talents to plug the talent and skills gap in the meantime.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In a February 2020 McKinsey article, it was reported that 87% of companies surveyed around the world say they are either experiencing manpower gaps now or expect to experience it within a few years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Respondents expect market and technology trends to play a big part in these shifts.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: More dramatically, the World Economic Forum describes the world as facing a "reskilling emergency".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Companies and countries are motivated to close the skills gap fast.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore needs to be even faster; one to two years' window of opportunity, according to some prominent business leaders in the ICT industry I encountered from within and outside of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Unresolved US-China tensions and rising protectionism around the world resulted in talent displacement.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Amongst these talents, there is a group which not only has deep skills, but also an international perspective, given their exposures.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we are able to tap on this group of talents and pick the "winners" for Singapore before others do, Singapore's transformation could be catalysed and more top enterprises with good jobs for our people will be attracted to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask what role is the Government playing in attracting talents to Singapore, for Singapore, as we strive towards our future economy?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ultimately, our Singaporean Core must benefit from this exercise and so, how could we ensure skills and knowledge transfer?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of these talents are founders of fast-rising startups or fast-growing firms.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Still, they can invest in Singapore and have a role to play in helping to develop our workforce.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Might the Government be exploring ways to harness the value they can offer to Singapore, and help groom our youths and talents, without requiring them to physically anchor here?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singapore is on track to fulfill our smart nation aspiration and is positioned to become a leader in AI and blockchain.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Big data fuels AI and AI will drive many daily applications in our digital future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, the quality and integrity of data is important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Having data that can readily be shared or used from one system to another is also important.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) integrates and transforms, and as Singapore champions the effort to build and strengthen the ASEAN Smart Cities Network, how do we ensure that the data generated are meaningful, of good quality and interoperable across the region?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What role can Singapore play in influencing and setting standards for the data and the digital infrastructure necessary for a smart ASEAN?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This development will see an "explosion" of data and the need for high speed processing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Data centres are, therefore, a critical infrastructure for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is the backbone of our future economy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How many data centres do we expect to be built and at what pace in order to achieve our smart nation and smart ASEAN aims?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Data centres worldwide generate 0.3% of carbon footprint today and is set to increase.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, what is the Government doing to promote greater efficiencies and mitigate the carbon footprints as we build more data centres?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How do we reconcile this expected increase in energy consumption and carbon footprints while achieving our target of halving carbon emissions by 2030 and zero by 2050?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: Mr Chairman, data can be used for great good or it can be used to inflict terrible harm.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: We need to address the issue of secondary acquisition of data and the use of legally acquired data by undesirable companies.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: For example, a foreign online company might acquire and transfer the personal data from a local company.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: These foreign online betting companies then target the vulnerable and entice them to gamble.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: How can the Minister ensure that data portability and data protection can work together without conflict?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: I would also like to ask the Minister how we can use legislation to restrict the data that companies collect.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: What users often encounter on websites or when downloading apps on their smartphones are these lengthy click-through agreements with a lot of information disclosure provisions embedded in those agreements.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: The result is that when the users click "accept", they are allowing these information disclosure terms which expose them to the sharing of data and often without their knowledge.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister what ethical safeguards can be put in place to protect the consumer and Singaporeans at large.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: These individuals are tasked with the responsibility of ensuring that the organisation complies with the Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Increasingly, companies and organisations have also realised that the job responsibilities of a data protection officer are often executive and managerial in nature, requiring the development and implementation of policies and processes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: All this should translate into more job openings for DPOs which would be suitable for PMETs looking to make this mid-career switch or to be redeployed in their existing organisations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Can MCI share how many new roles and job openings this will possibly create for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Notwithstanding, to facilitate the successful hiring, placement and redeployment of PMETs in the data protection field, there is a need to take more active steps to train, place, match and redeploy suitable PMETs to potential employers, or even data protection and compliance roles within their existing organisations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It was developed to guide data protection professionals in enhancing their competencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: It also provides guidance on the viable career pathways for different levels of DPOs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I hope to hear MCI's plans on what and how we can do more to make this area of expertise an attractive and viable option for mid-career PMETs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, we have seen an increase in the application of facial recognition technologies being employed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Even this House is contemplating the use of this technology to track Members' attendance.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While this technology started out mainly to tackle security, are there any guidelines for the use of facial recognition technology to ensure data is not misused for commercial purposes and that its use does not compromise personal data security?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, several buildings, such as the United Overseas Bank (UOB) Plaza and Singapore Exchange (SGX) Centre, already use such technology.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The use of facial recognition for building access would link the name of the visitor to the facial recognition data.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Does facial recognition data then become part of the intellectual property (IP) of the technology vendor?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How long can the vendor keep such information?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the vendor use the same information for its other customers?

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The other aspect is whether the vendor is allowed to link facial recognition pattern to even more data, such as consumer buying behaviour.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The possible abuse of such technology is mindboggling if we do not have guidelines on its use.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Where exceptions are needed, express consent should be obtained and, even then, there should always be a maximum time limit for which facial recognition data can be stored.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Chairman, it is a brave new world that we live in and I am worried that, without guidelines, there will be misuse of facial recognition technology and data.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I really hope that MCI can look into this issue.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Mohamed Irshad, take both your cuts, please.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, globally, the post and parcel industry is undoubtedly being disrupted.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: With ever-changing returns in core mail business, the rapid take-up of e-commerce and shifting customer expectations, post and parcel companies of today need to be adaptable, they need to be relevant and to be innovative to keep pace with changing demands.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Many consumers have also increased expectations about the convenience and options offered by deliveries and postal infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Today, there are only several logistics service providers that offer last-mile delivery services besides SingPost.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, what are the Government's plans to transform our domestic postal infrastructure to meet these new demands, ensuring world-class delivery standards?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, what can consumers and businesses look forward to in the future and how will these changes be integrated with the current postal infrastructure in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I turn to speak about fifth generation (5G) – 5G is the basis for digital connectivity and will be the backbone for our digital future.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: It will enable possible new areas of growth in autonomous vehicles, and the Internet of Things in industry and in consumer segments.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: What is the Government doing to support the rollout of 5G to ensure that Singapore remains competitive on the international front?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, how will 5G benefit Singaporeans and ensure that 5G remains affordable for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, as Singapore prepares to roll out the 5G network this year, there are companies that are concerned about the security measures of 5G deployment.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister provide by way of an update how ready is Singapore to embrace 5G communication networks and what plans are in place to help enterprises understand and exploit this technology to its fullest while managing its challenges?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Ministry have any plans to engage Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs) to help understand from businesses what they would most need from such a new technology and to implement the new technological equipment and applications?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, we often do not realise how widespread and important digitisation is in our lives.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of the most important digital spaces are what we refer to as the critical information infrastructure (CII) which our national Cyber Security Agency (CSA) has been set up to safeguard.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: CII currently includes the critical data used for sectors, such as aviation, healthcare, land transport, maritime, media, security and emergency, water, banking and finance, Government and energy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Data is necessary to keep our power plants, hospitals, water, banks and even Government functioning smoothly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The more we digitise and automate, the more important our CII becomes and the greater the risk we face of something going wrong here.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This survey covered staff in the utilities, energy, health and transport sectors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This report also concluded that a lack of resources and intelligence about the “relentless and continuous” cyberattacks are the industry’s concern.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The key points from this study were that we have to assume attacks will be made and be prepared to deal with them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We also need to be able to guard against human failings, and this may include employees accidentally opening phishing emails and thereby opening the network to attack.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There is also a need to share intelligence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe the national CSA is focusing on these matters and I would be interested in an update on how the Government is safeguarding the cybersecurity and resilience of our CII.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One, to strengthen the resilience of our CII; two, to mobilise businesses and the community to make cyberspace safe; three, to develop a vibrant cybersecurity ecosystem comprising a skilled workforce, technologically advanced companies and strong research collaborations; and four, to step up efforts to forge strong international partnerships.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since 2016, much has happened to focus us on our cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, CSA's mandate enables it to direct owners of CII on the essential cybersecurity measures to be adopted and to provide professional consultancy and direct assistance to them, where necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How does CSA ensure that its officers have the necessary expertise to devise credible regulations and guidelines?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is particularly needed in vendor management as it is common for data owners to outsource data management to third-party providers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I now move on to a query on the role of CSA vis-a-vis the public sector.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the Cybersecurity Act regime, owners of CII include the Government, as it is running various essential services.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Last year, the Government convened a public sector data security review committee which recently issued its report on enhancing public sector data security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister clarify what CSA played in this review?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: Furthermore, 93% of these organisations reported an increase in cyberattacks in the past year.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: The report added that 98% of chief information officers and chief information security officers surveyed were concerned how digital transformation projects and the rollout of the 5G network will further affect cybersecurity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: More than 250 chief information officers, chief technology officers and chief information security officers from across a range of sectors participated in this survey .

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: According to a study by consumer information provider, Comparitech, which studied 60 countries based on criteria, such as percentage of mobiles and computers infected with malware and the number of attacks by cryptominers in 2018, Singapore ranked 10th place in global cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: This is commendable, but reports on probable attacks, such as the personal data leak of Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) and Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) staff in December 2019 is still a cause for concern.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: Taking an analogy from the health perspective, our previous experience with the Severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) taught us the importance of having a readily adoptable response framework, such that today, Singapore’s Disease Outbreak Response System Condition (DORSCON) framework has been widely praised in the handling of the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Over the past two to three decades, digital computing technologies have rapidly changed the world, with far ranging implications on businesses and consumers.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Particularly, the pace of adoption of digital technologies have accelerated over the last decade.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Adoption of digital technologies has resulted in a very connected world, empowering individuals and transforming how consumers, businesses and governments operate.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Today, there are many Smart Nation applications which allow accessibility at any time and, thus, bring significant conveniences to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: At the enterprise level, operational technology (OT) allows the direct monitoring and control of critical plants, power and telecommunication grids.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: It yields significant control and productivity benefits, including preventive maintenance, reducing downtime and quality control, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: OT is expected to assume an expanding role in government and many organisations, enabling greater integration among business processes, physical activities and supporting technology.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: I would like to ask the Minister how we ensure that the Government and enterprises here can be better protected against this new threat.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: And how has CSA been contributing to this effort?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Dozens of protestors in a Ukrainian town attacked buses carrying 72 evacuees from Wuhan, China, enroute to a quarantine facility in Ukraine.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: These demonstrators lighted bonfires and hurled stones in clashes with police officers and national guards.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Even armoured personnel carriers were deployed to this small town.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: The protest was started because of a hoax – a fake email claiming to be from the Ukrainian Health Ministry, falsely claiming that some evacuees had contracted the virus.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Indeed, many observers have commented that the challenges of COVID-19 is not just in containing the "biological virus" but also in containing the "psychological fear and irrationality", and this often arise from fake news and rumours.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: These and many other examples of fake news have been circulating around, threatening to undermine our national effort and public trust in addressing the COVID-19 situation.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Chairman, there were also discussions in this House that judges should be the body issuing Correction Notices under POFMA, as opposed to Ministers.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Do our recent experiences of implementing POFMA to deal with the outbreak, like the current COVID-19 situation, reinforce the Government's position that the issuance of Correction Notices is, indeed, a job best left to the Executive branch?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: POFMA has served to preserve the stability by dealing with false information.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: But it is also important to ensure that our citizens have access to trusted information.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon
text: I would also like to ask the Minister whether he would consider to drop the paywall on The Straits Times during times of emergency.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, in as much as COVID-19 has been an abominable threat, it has also been an illuminating lesson on the importance of effective communication and the importance of a robust information infrastructure.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Just as medical care has improved significantly since SARS, information and communication technologies have also seen considerable transformations.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Our information landscape is paradoxically more fragmented, yet more connected at the same time.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: It is fragmented and balkanised because there is a plethora of information and communication channels out there.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from traditional mainstream media that is actively seeking to digitalise, we now have access to vastly more online content across a range of different platforms, including WhatsApp, Telegram, WeChat, Facebook and TikTok.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, very difficult to capture in any parsimonious way the chequered universe of information that audiences today consume and are influenced by.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Despite this seeming fragmentation, our information landscape is concurrently more connected because of growing ownership of personal media devices, such as smartphones.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Individual consumers across the world are thus linked to one another online, creating content and sharing it across platforms, geographical boundaries and even linguistic barriers now being rapidly eroded by translation software.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In a globalised hyper-connected world, our understanding of local situations is thus enriched but also complicated by perspectives extending far beyond our immediate environments.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: As media consumers, we must contend not only with domestic information flows but manage the onslaught of international news, quite apart from having to discern between legitimate news and false rumours.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: In such a fraught media landscape, rumours and falsehoods can become virulent social contagions that trigger mob mentality and herd behaviour like the panic buying we experienced and are now witnessing in North America.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, our public agencies managing our official communications cannot afford to be insular and track only local discourse around crises of a global nature.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, can we obtain data from the Internet intermediaries on the reach and access of the corrections that have been issued so that we may ascertain the effectiveness of the corrections strategy and finetune it accordingly?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, we must seize the opportunity to survey consumers to comprehend how they have managed the onslaught of falsehoods that they have received in light of COVID-19.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: What personal measures have they taken to verify the information they have received about the disease?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Did they use services, such as the gov.sg WhatsApp chat and Factually, and how did they perceive them?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: How did they react when they encountered suspected falsehoods that had not been issued with POFMA orders?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Did they subsequently assume that these falsehoods were true, thereby developing unhealthy cognitive shortcuts?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: These are all crucial questions that we must answer to strengthen both our official communication strategies and our public education efforts.

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: Might it not make better sense in the long run to use existing apps, such as SGSecure, for official Government alerts during periods of crisis?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: While I understand that SGSecure was launched and is managed by the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), should our whole-of-Government approach not predispose us to more strategically integrate our multiple communication channels that we have?

speaker: Prof Lim Sun Sun (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome clarifications on the concerns I have raised.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Chairman, the COVID-19 crisis has shown that there is a need for accurate, timely and trusted public communications between the Government and the people in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: It is important that the Government provide accurate and timely information to different segments of society to allay public anxieties.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Unfortunately, in a situation of information vacuum, distortions, rumours, untruths, misinformation and smears can undermine public confidence and be divisive.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Second, what are the public communications efforts undertaken by the Government to update Singaporeans on COVID-19?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Has the Government tried anything new or different?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: Are we expecting any improvements along the way to improve our crisis-response handling?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: And will the Government review the effectiveness of these efforts, especially in the realm of misinformation?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad
text: To me, it seems like a simple way to ensure that we can provide timely and verified information to our people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Digitisation is all around us, making our life simpler and more convenient.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As a Smart Government, numerous Government services are now available online and on smartphone apps.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: And everything from taxes to parking payments can be done with a few clicks on one's phone.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Other services like banking, credit card bill payments and even food delivery can be done in the comfort of one's armchair.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, the darker side of information is that misinformation is also freely sent and communicated, through social media and messaging tools, such as WhatsApp.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: There have been numerous examples of this, the most recent being the COVID-19 outbreak which my colleagues, Mr Ong Teng Koon, Mr Cedric Foo and Mr Mohamed Irshad, have elaborated on.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Another area of concern is scams, which really target more vulnerable residents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I, myself, have been subject to a phone call from an Australian phone number claiming to be from Singtel's technical staff.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: I happened to be at my computer and having attended all the grassroots sessions on scams, quickly googled Singtel scams and discovered that this was actually a well-documented scam and stopped that call.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In fact, I have personally become so skeptical that if someone calls me telling me they represent my bank, I will usually say I will call the bank myself, rather than reveal any personal data.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, many others may be more trusting and it is the trusting who get exploited by these scams.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: But I would be interested to know if the Government is taking any steps to help individuals themselves become safe, informed and more discerning online.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, as we have heard from my Parliamentary colleagues speaking before me, the outbreak of COVID-19 has once again shone the spotlight on the dangers of fake news and their negative impact on social cohesion and trust.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Governments around the world are combating the daily deluge of fake news on COVID-19, and Singapore was also not spared.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fake news, such as the shutting down of MRT stations and certain shopping malls, closure of schools and rumoured deaths, sparked social panic and, in some cases, xenophobic reactions against certain communities and restaurants.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The deluge of fake news has undermined the ability of governments worldwide to manage the COVID-19 epidemic.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, the World Health Organization (WHO) went as far as to label fake coronavirus claims as an "infodemic" that threatens the management of the outbreak.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To manage the "infodemic", a WHO representative met tech firms in Silicon Valley recently to urge them through moral suasion to do more to combat the spread of fake news and deliberate false information.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even though we have taken on a less harsh approach than other countries in this instance, the truth is that online falsehoods and untruths in general will continue to be a scourge, a scourge to our community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would thus like to ask how the Government can continue to help Singaporeans guard against deliberate online falsehoods in an increasingly complex digital and media environment.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The growing popularity of over-the-top (OTT) media services has led to a worldwide decline in viewership rating amongst free-to-air (FTA) television (TV) channels.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This cuts across all demographics and implies that, over time, fewer people will be exposed to Public Service Broadcasting (PSB) messages from FTA TV channels and that the Government will need to explore other channels, other platforms and other medium to share these messages with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How is Public Service Broadcasting remaining relevant, given the increasing competition for eyeballs from online and foreign platforms?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, the consumption of media has shifted from over-the-air broadcasting services to OTT services that I mentioned in my previous cut.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These OTT services offer media content directly to consumers via Internet streaming, bypassing cable, broadcast and even satellite TV platforms that were traditional distributors of media content.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Furthermore, the availability of OTT services also mean that consumers today have a greater variety of media content to choose from and are exposed to a wider range of media options from beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This shift in media consumption pattern has brought about disruptions to the local media scene as our local media providers need to adapt quickly to offer a greater variety of original content over non-traditional platforms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would thus like to ask what plans the Government has to develop and support the local media industry in this evolving media environment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Access to and decisions based on timely and accurate information are important to any democracy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Singaporeans should have access to accurate information in forms that they can easily understand.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: For a long time, it was highly challenging for older Singaporeans, many of whom were not English educated, to consume Government information as collaterals were typically in the English language.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Only selected material, such as Central Provident Fund letters come in different languages.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: To the Government's credit, the situation has improved significantly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: Therefore, what is the Government doing to ensure timely and inclusive access to all Government-related information by all Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling
text: How might the advancement of technology complement this effort?

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, in the initial days when I set up offices overseas, whether it is China, Kuala Lumpur or Jakarta, I used a translator for the local contracts as well as for meetings.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lately, I have been using online platforms, especially in China and also in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The online platforms that they produce locally enable me to do translation in double-quick time.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because it not only enhances individuals in terms of translating the languages and also the meaning of certain words across different cultures and across different languages, it will also enhance or enable businesses to be able to conduct its business in different languages as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Ser Luck (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, I wanted to ask the Ministry whether it has such plans to be able to put up that online platform or to merge technology with languages.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, to be a Smart Nation, it is important to first build a smart infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Subsequently, it is important that such be made accessible to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, not all users have data plans which will enable them to fully and freely use their smart mobile devices and mobile app services.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The costs of subscription of these mobile data plans are an impediment to creating a Smart Nation.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The speed at which we educate our smart mobile device users is another barrier, slowing our progress to becoming a digital society.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will encourage lifelong learning and active digital lifestyles among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Chairman, my cut is on the future role of our public libraries.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Traditional paper	books	are gradually	being	replaced	by electronic	books.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: This trend is not unique to the US and is rather common amongst most developed countries.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: It is particularly pronounced amongst younger readers and, increasingly so, younger readers have voiced their preference for reading from electronic devices.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Many adults, including Singaporean adults, are no longer visiting the library to pick up paper books as they did in the past.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: The possibilities are exciting and we are eager to hear from the Minister on his views about the future role of our libraries.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, may I have your permission to display a few slides?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It has been an eventful year for MCI, not least because of viruses, both biological and digital.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want to thank all Members who have spoken and posed their questions, queries and suggestions for my Ministry.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Several Members have spoken on the unprecedented and pervasive impact of digitalisation, as well as the exciting new opportunities it brings for our economy, our workers and our people.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Digital technology not only enhances enterprise productivity but also creates novel pathways to access new markets.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Exciting careers are emerging in both ICT and non-ICT sectors in digital marketing, data analytics and AI.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We, therefore, have good reasons to be optimistic about our digital future.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, the promise of digitalisation is tempered by the uncertainty of change and the fear of disruption to businesses, jobs and even our lives.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Enterprises, particularly SMEs, worry that they would not be able to keep pace with digitalisation and risked being marginalised.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some, including mid-career professionals, feel the long-term implications of new technologies like AI.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The less tech-savvy amongst our citizens are concerned that they are on the wrong side of a digital divide that is ever widening.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Moreover, a persistent strain of online misinformation and falsehoods threatens to erode trust in our institutions and, ultimately, our democracy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These are real concerns and they must be effectively addressed so that every business, every worker and every citizen has the assurance and the deep conviction that they, too, can thrive in a digital future.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that is the mission of my Ministry – to work with all Singaporeans to build a digital future where there are opportunities for all, where no one is left behind, and where trust in our institutions is preserved.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In this Committee of Supply (COS) debate, Senior Minister of State Sim Ann, Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary and I, in responding to Members' queries, will elaborate on how MCI is working on three broad thrusts to forge our digital future together by seizing digital opportunities, ensuring a digital future for all and securing our digital spaces.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Cedric Foo has asked about our plans to enter into digital trade agreements and facilitate digital transactions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Chairman, digital is the new frontier for trade, with cross border flows growing exponentially.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And just as we did for international trade in goods and service, Singapore is now actively involved in shaping the international rules and norms that will govern digital trade.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I also want to assure Mr Douglas Foo that in undertaking these negotiations on DEAs, our Government agencies regularly consult our business interests, business agencies and organisations, in order to establish their interests and ensure that they are adequately captured and reflected in these DEAs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We also need to foster trust in digital systems by building an international consensus on ethical and governance principles for nascent technologies and system threats.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: At this juncture, Mr Chairman, I want to hasten to add that MCI is not the progenitor of the idea of using facial recognition in Parliament.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Chairman, I think you are better-placed in that.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Singapore has been an active participant in international platforms to shape global norms in cybersecurity and AI governance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In cybersecurity, Singapore actively participates in the United Nations (UN) Open-Ended Working Group and the 25-member Group of Government Experts, to develop a rules-based cyberspace and to implement norms for responsible state behaviour.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Earlier this year, I also launched the second edition of our Model AI Governance Framework at the World Economic Forum meeting in Davos.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The framework translates broad governance principles into practical guidelines for businesses which are implementing AI solutions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Notably, diverse organisations, from Omada Health in San Francisco, to our Development Bank of Singapore (DBS) Bank and Pymetrics, a human resource (HR) solutions provider, have adopted the best practices in the Model Framework.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, in other words, it is gaining recognition, acceptance and traction.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Seizing digital opportunities also requires world-class infrastructure and I would like to highlight two important initiatives in this regard.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The first is 5G, which will be the backbone of our digital economy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are committed to building a world-class, secure and resilient 5G network in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that is why network design, resilience and security have been key requirements in IMDA's 5G Call for Proposal (CFP), which was launched last October.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Government is also collaborating with industry partners, a point that both Mr Douglas Foo and Mr Mohamad Irshad have raised, to develop our 5G ecosystem, learn from early trials for future development application and position Singapore at the forefront of global innovation in 5G applications and services.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Mohamad Irshad asked about the status of 5G rollout in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Douglas Foo and Mr Mohamad Irshad have also asked about the benefit and cost of 5G.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The initial deployment is expected to be in certain industry sectors and consumer applications where there is keen interest to explore innovative 5G use cases.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, PSA has had promising results in using 5G technology to control its Automated Guided Vehicles and automated cranes, in another step towards realising its vision of being a Smart Port.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In terms of cost, similar to 3G and 4G services, the cost of service plans and handsets are expected to moderate as the technology matures.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Mohamad Irshad has also asked how we are modernising our logistics networks.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is an important point because driven by e-commerce growth, parcel deliveries have grown rapidly worldwide.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The network will be owned by IMDA and accessible to all logistics players.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It will offer greater choice to consumers, while raising the productivity of the urban logistics sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will further elaborate on the national parcel locker network initiative.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The goal of our DEAs and investment in world-class infrastructure is to benefit all our businesses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we are helping our companies, especially our SMEs, adopt digital solutions through IMDA's now well-known SMEs Go Digital initiative.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A recent SBF survey found that 94% of enterprises recognise the importance of digital technology in transforming businesses.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, the awareness is high and that is a starting point from which we can work.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But we can do more, especially to help our enterprises scale and access global markets through digital channels, as emphasised by Ms Rahayu Mahzam and Mr Ong Teng Koon.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, IMDA is launching a new initiative, under the overarching SMEs Go Digital, and it is called Grow Digital, which will help SMEs access overseas opportunities without the need to establish an in-market physical presence.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: By connecting to business-to-business (B2B) and business-to-consumer (B2C) e-commerce platforms, our SMEs will benefit from smart matching with potential overseas clients, prompt access to financing offers through the platforms and integration with logistics companies for last-mile delivery.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Grow Digital will also help SMEs fully utilise Singapore's network of free trade agreements (FTAs) and our DEAs to extend their business linkages and grow their customer base.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: More broadly, IMDA will continue to work with Government agencies and other stakeholders on the Industry Digital Plans (IDPs) for various sectors, such as sea transport, food services and accountancy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These IDPs guide SMEs on the digital solutions and training available at each stage of their digital journey and growth.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: IMDA and Enterprise Singapore (ESG) launched the Food Services IDP in November 2018.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A Nielsen study commissioned by ESG last year found that Food Services SMEs which had adopted digital solutions found them easy to implement, which is important, and 70% of these companies have seen shorter waiting times and greater satisfaction for customers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Through these IDPs, SMEs in sectors, such as construction, food manufacturing and adult and early childhood education, will benefit from dedicated digital roadmaps to help transform their business and upskill their workers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ultimately, this array of initiatives I have outlined to help our businesses make the digital transformation must yield benefits and opportunities for our people.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We know that digital disruption can cause profound anxiety for mature workers, especially those who may be more advanced in their careers and not have a technology background.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They are, in fact, the focus of the Next Bound of SkillsFuture that Deputy Prime Minister Heng Swee Keat announced in the Budget.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We want to pay special attention to these mid-career workers, many of whom are in their 40s and 50s, and most keenly feel the uncertainty caused by technological disruption, but they also stand to gain from the new jobs that are being created if the opportunity is presented and they have the requisite skills.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Kevin Lee, who went through Company-Led Training (CLT) under TeSA, is an example.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Lee used to be a senior executive in sales and marketing at several leading technology MNCs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, he was doing non-tech business in tech companies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: After nine months of "deep-skilling" with AI Singapore, he is now an AI consultant, helping organisations figure out how best to use AI and machine learning technologies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, this is an important part of what we are doing with our mature workers already, but Ms Tin Pei Ling and Mr Ong Teng Koon have asked what more we can do, especially for mature workers and those who do not have a tech background.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The TechSkills Accelerator (TeSA) programme is a tripartite effort between Government agencies, industry and the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) to equip workers with digital skills and place them in good jobs in the ICT sector.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: IMDA works with trade associations like SG Tech to raise awareness of TeSA.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: SMEs also qualify for higher levels of funding support, especially for certain types of short-form training programmes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The employers value and the employees get a job that they are able to secure and work from.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As part of the next bound for TeSA, IMDA is piloting a new programme, TeSA Mid-Career Advance, for professionals aged 40 and above.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our aim is to lessen the friction that gets in the way of mature workers being able to benefit from opportunities being created in tech sectors or the fast-growing tech areas.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We expect to create in the ICT and ICM sectors over 20,000 jobs in the next two to three years.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We want, on the one hand, to make it easier for employers to bring these workers into their team, lessening some of the initial costs that might get in the way, and, at the same time, enable workers to bridge into these roles with the appropriate training.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Under TeSA Mid-Career Advance, the Government will support companies to hire and train mid-career professionals for tech-related jobs, regardless of whether they have an ICT background.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Participating companies will benefit from access to a bigger pool of local talent as well as Government subsidies to partially offset the cost of the training and the salaries for the duration of the training.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The mid-career individual will benefit from employment in a growth sector while gaining exposure, training and mentorship for up to 24 months.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ten companies have already come on board and they have committed to about 500 positions covering many roles, both tech and tech-lite, from data analysts, cybersecurity engineers and cloud computing engineers, to business analysts, project managers and sales specialists.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Cedric Foo and Ms Tin Pei Ling have also asked how we will address the need to augment our local talent pipeline with the requisite talent from abroad in selected, emerging fields.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Government recognises that tech companies in Singapore and others whom we want to attract need specialists from overseas in certain fields.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why we have programmes like Tech@SG, which provides fast-growth tech companies with access to business networks and talent, so as to build their teams in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In addition, our economic agencies, like the Economic Development Board (EDB), IMDA and the Digital Industry Singapore (DISG), are working with the tech companies largely, work closely with them and see how they can be helped to secure the talent that is needed to complement the local pool and enable them to execute their strategies competitively.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In addition, and I think this goes to the point that Ms Tin Pei Ling raised, IMDA and WSG help our companies to leverage this specialised expertise from abroad to develop new skillsets amongst Singaporeans, in other words, a transfer of capability, through the Capability Transfer Programme.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is a conscious part of this effort, even as we bring in talent from abroad to complement our local talent base.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Before I move away from the topic of talent, Mr Cedric Foo raised the point about what is happening in our universities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The details and the more complete response will be given in the Ministry of Education (MOE) COS debate, but I think it would suffice for me to say that both in terms of quantity and quality, the intakes for the courses pertaining to computer science and so on have been rising.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We see this as being a very rich pipeline that will then enter the industry and meet its needs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Beyond jobs and businesses, as more citizens embrace technology to enrich their lives or access public services, we must make sure that no one feels outpaced by the change or left behind.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann will explain how we are increasing support for low-income households, seniors and children to ensure our digital future is an inclusive one.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In this mission, our libraries also have a very important role.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Our libraries epitomise the spirit of the SG Together movement, bringing our people, volunteers and partners together in a supportive learning environment.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Over the next several months, the National Library Board (NLB) will be engaging with various communities, partners and stakeholders on its future strategies, collections and services to ensure that it continues to meet the needs and aspirations of Singaporeans in an evolving learning and knowledge landscape.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Cedric Foo has asked how we ensure that we are adequately protected in this environment.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also raised some questions pertaining to CSA and the work we do with the CII.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Cybersecurity is key, in particular, to safeguard our CII from cyber threats.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: CSA has been conducting regular reviews as well as exercises with the 11 CII sectors and the component agencies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But as Members can well appreciate, this is an iterative and ongoing process, because the threats keep evolving and, therefore, our capacity to deal with them must also keep evolving in tandem.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will elaborate on MCI's new measures to enhance cybersecurity and data security.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But we do have to go beyond cybersecurity and data protection because, ultimately, our aim is to uphold the values of our society, the strength of our institutions and preserve our common spaces.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Today, the online space is where our hard-won cohesion could fray and splinter.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the digital age, our common spaces are no longer just physical.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is where our laws against online falsehoods become very important, a point that Mr Darryl David has asked.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: POFMA has been used to place factual corrections next to the grievous falsehoods which distorted or fabricated facts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These falsehoods have pertained to the COVID-19 situation, Police procedures and the management of public funds, among other things.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If Singaporeans are duped into believing such falsehoods, it can sow fear, cause panic and erode trust in our institutions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why, in response, we have used the powers under POFMA to juxtapose the truth with the falsehoods at the source, so that our citizens can see both and draw their own conclusions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In this fight against online falsehoods, it is heartening to see Singaporeans stepping up to do their part.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Amid many online rumours that have been circulating in the context of COVID-19, a group of students from Nanyang Technological University (NTU) started a fact-checking initiative called "Sure Anot" – a bit of Singlish there – aimed at older Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They developed a guide for seniors to assess information they receive, based on NLB's digital literacy framework of "Source, Understand, Research, Evaluate".

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They also collaborated with an independent fact-checking outfit to share reports of debunked rumours in Facebook and WhatsApp groups.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In a similar vein, I am also glad to share with Members that there are many initiatives from academia to study the challenges of the online information ecosystem.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In particular, the National University of Singapore (NUS) is setting up a Centre for Trusted Internet and Community that will drive research and strengthen public discourse on the impact of the Internet and online harms.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Senior Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will share the details.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: All these strands of work to sustain trust and cohesion through information and communications were put to the test when the COVID-19 virus broke out.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon, Mr Mohamad Irshad and Prof Lim Sun Sun have all asked about the lessons learnt from the experience.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Cedric Foo has asked specifically about the role that POFMA played in dealing with falsehoods about the virus.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: COVID-19 is not a medical and public health challenge, it is also a psychological battle against fear and uncertainty.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong put it, "Fear can actually do more harm than the virus itself".

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Government has, therefore, sought to allay the fears of our citizens and keep their trust by being transparent about the situation, the measures we are taking and the reasons for doing so, and giving regular information on the evolving situation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Some have caused anxiety in our population by putting out falsehoods.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is abundantly clear that it would have been much harder to quell the spread of misinformation and keep the calm of our society without this set of POFMA measures, which are designed specifically to address falsehoods in the online space.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But to focus only on the use of POFMA for COVID-19 would be to miss the wood for the trees.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: MCI has also conducted a major public communication and education campaign through the print and broadcast mainstream media, Government websites and social media.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Alas, removing The Straits Times' paywall is beyond my ken, but I do hope that the relevant people will heed Mr Ong Teng Koon's plaintive call and do the necessary.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have collaborated with Mediacorp and local celebrities in all four official languages and also in dialects, such as Hokkien, Teochew, Cantonese, Hakka and Hainanese.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This communication campaign would have been much more challenging if we did not have the national platforms with the content and reach to engage and connect with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Darryl David asked how Public Service Broadcasting (PSB) will remain relevant amid the changing landscape.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: PSB has long been a key source of trusted information and common experiences.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But with these changes in media landscape, we know that Singaporeans enjoy access to multiple media platforms but it is imperative that they also continue to access local content that reflects and strengthens our national voice and character.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Prof Lim Sun Sun has asked whether we can take a more strategic approach and integrate the multiple communications channels onto existing Government mobile apps like SG Secure.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In today’s fragmented media landscape, we have to bring the information to our people through the different platforms that they rely on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The diversity of channels is, therefore, an inevitable consequence.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I want to assure Prof Lim Sun Sun that, as part of MCI's ongoing efforts, we are working with Smart Nation Digital Office (SNDGO) and other agencies to see how we can further integrate and coordinate these different channels.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But we should not let that overarching objective get in the way of responding to needs as they emerge, as they did in recent times with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Already, amid the COVID-19 situation, our efforts have cut through new digital platforms.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This broad-based Government communication effort has been recognised and appreciated by our citizens and many others.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we are getting through, communicating, but we can always do better.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to conclude by going back to where I began.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is clear that the digital future holds much promise for Singapore but there are real concerns over the impact of technology on our enterprises and jobs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Be it investment in world-class infrastructure to seize digital opportunities, ensuring digital opportunities for all by helping our mid-career professionals secure jobs in the growing ICT sector, or education and enforcement to strengthen the digital defence of our common spaces, our goal is to forge a digital future where our businesses have the abilities and capabilities to thrive, our workers have good jobs with the requisite skills, and our citizens lead fulfilling lives by embracing emerging digital technologies.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And MCI is resolutely committed to working together with all Singaporeans to forge this digital vision for our nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Chairman, digitalisation can bring greater convenience, efficiency, participation and better services for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A secure digital infrastructure will be important to allow our citizens to live safely, work productively and enjoy themselves online.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Cedric Foo, Mr Vikram Nair and Ms Sylvia Lim asked about the Government's efforts on cybersecurity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: CSA has been working to protect our CIIs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This is the first pillar of Singapore’s cybersecurity strategy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These systems are critical for providing essential services, like energy and water.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Since the SingHealth Committee of Inquiry (COI) concluded a year ago, CSA has worked with CII sector leads to strengthen their defences and to implement the Committee’s recommendations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to track their progress and enable the further implementation of these measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is crucial to strengthen our defences on operational technology (OT) systems as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These are systems that control physical and industrial processes and manufacturing equipment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As many of the CIIs rely on these, attacks on OT systems can cause physical disruption.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Douglas Foo asked if Singapore has a cyber response framework similar to the DORSCON Framework used to handle COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are broad similarities in how we respond.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: CSA has a framework to calibrate the approach to mitigate potential threats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Should there be an incident of concern, this framework also helps us to coordinate an appropriate national response to secure our cyberspace, a response that will involve multiple stakeholders and agencies as well as private sector entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Similar to containing COVID-19, in cybersecurity, we need processes to give us an early warning and a multi-stakeholder approach to mitigate any impact of a large-scale cyberattack.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We do this by ensuring timely information sharing from multiple sources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Under the Cybersecurity Act, CII owners are required to monitor systems and report incidents to CSA.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: CSA then works closely with industry and international partners to share cyber intelligence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: However, we must plan on the basis that we cannot prevent all cyber incidents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Determined attackers will always find new ways to breach our systems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, we must be vigilant and be prepared to respond to and recover quickly from any attack.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To these ends, CSA conducts regular exercises, such as Exercise Cyber Star, to prepare the nation in the event of a widespread cyberattack.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As part of Singapore’s Cybersecurity Strategy, the Government also works with businesses and the general public to improve their cybersecurity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For example, SingCERT provides regular advisories about identified vulnerabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Beyond the CIIs, CSA will continue to expand broad efforts to protect cyberspace through the new Safer Cyberspace Masterplan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This aims to make Singapore one of the most cyber-secure countries in the world, benefiting all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The plan involves, firstly, securing Singapore’s digital core; secondly, safeguarding activities in cyberspace; and thirdly, empowering a cyber-savvy population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Details on this Safer Cyberspace Masterplan will be announced later in the year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: A growing area of concern is the Internet of Things (IoT).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This refers to devices, like home routers, smart home hubs, which many of us may have in our homes and offices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We expect that the number of these devices will grow significantly as they become more and more useful.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Communications and Information (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
